Nutrition is more than a healthy or unhealthy label.

Everyday foods hide trade-offs. Some are calorie dense, some bring protein with extra fat, and some categories look similar until you compare the nutrients side by side.

What the data asks us to notice

People often judge food from a single signal: calories, sugar, fat, or a familiar category name. This narrative lets you filter, compare, hover, and click through the data so those assumptions become testable.

Guiding question

Which foods offer the nutrition you want, and what trade-offs come with them?

    Step 6

    Real-life meaning

    For younger people, the story is often about growth, energy, and learning how foods differ. For adults, the same data can support choices around long-term health, weight management, heart disease risk, and diabetes risk.

    Teens

    Focus on growth, steady energy, protein, iron, and vitamin C instead of judging foods by calories alone.

    Young adults

    Compare foods that fit busy schedules while balancing protein, calories, fat, and useful micronutrients.

    Adults

    Compare several measures at once, especially when managing fat, carbs, and calorie density.

    Older adults

    Look for nutrient-dense foods that keep protein and micronutrients visible without letting calories dominate.

    Final takeaway

    Nutrition is more complex than simple labels.

    Making informed decisions requires comparing multiple factors at once. This is especially important across different age groups, because nutritional needs and health risks change over time, from growth and development in younger individuals to managing conditions like obesity, heart disease, or diabetes in adults. By interacting with the data, users can walk away with a clearer understanding of how to evaluate food choices based on their own priorities and make decisions that support their overall health.
